openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Long-term pressure on e5 and a slow queenside bind; strong for White strategically, but Black is fully sound and the theory runs deep.

positions.title: Ruy Lopez: keep the bishop
positions.prompt: Black has attacked your bishop. Keep it on the a4-e8 diagonal in this Closed Ruy Lopez line.
positions.explanation: Ba4 preserves the bishop and its pressure on c6. Bxc6 is a different opening choice, the Exchange Variation, rather than an illegal move.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Quiet build-up aiming the bishop at f7 and a later d4 break; easy to play and low-risk, but hands Black comfortable equality if White is unambitious.
notes: Claims the centre and opens lines for both the queen and the light bishop. The most played first move in chess.
Black copies the idea: an equal share of the centre, and the same pieces get free.
Develops a knight toward the centre and attacks e5 immediately. Knights usually come out before bishops.
Defends e5 with a developing move rather than a pawn move. Every move should ideally do a job and bring a piece out.
Points the bishop at f7. That square is defended only by the king, which is why so many early attacks aim there.
Black mirrors, eyeing f2 for the same reason.
A small move with a big idea: it supports playing d4 next, so White can build the full centre.
Develops and attacks e4 at the same time. Notice Black has castled nothing yet but every move has developed something.
Defends e4 quietly and keeps a solid centre. The plan from here is simple: castle, then finish developing before starting anything.

positions.title: Italian: prepare the centre
positions.prompt: Prepare a later d4 pawn break while keeping the Italian bishop active.
positions.explanation: c3 supports d4. White can build the centre after securing e4 and the king; the pawn break need not happen immediately.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black invites sharp play (4.Ng5 hitting f7) rather than symmetry; double-edged and tactical, rewarding the better-prepared side.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Opens the centre early for quick development and space; sidesteps heavy Ruy theory, but the early trade eases Black development too.
notes: Claims the centre and frees both the queen and the light bishop in one move.
Black stakes an equal claim rather than letting White own the middle of the board.
Develops toward the centre and attacks e5 at the same time, so the move does two jobs at once.
Defends e5 by bringing out a piece. Defending with a piece rather than a pawn keeps your position flexible.
The Scotch. White strikes at the centre straight away instead of the slower Italian or Spanish build-up.
Black should take: leaving the tension usually just loses the e5 pawn.
Recapturing with the knight puts it on a strong central square and keeps development flowing.

Black develops and hits e4. The position is open and symmetrical-ish, so whoever finishes developing and castles first tends to stand better. That simplicity is why the Scotch is a good first e4 opening to learn.

positions.title: Scotch: open the centre
positions.prompt: Challenge the e5 pawn now and open lines for your pieces.
positions.explanation: d4 strikes at e5. After ...exd4, Nxd4 recaptures with an active knight. This is the central idea of the Scotch.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black counterattacks symmetrically for a rock-solid, drawish game; very hard to crack, but concedes White easy equality and few winning chances for Black.

positions.title: Petroff: respond before recapturing
positions.prompt: White has taken on e5. Challenge that knight before recovering the e4 pawn.
positions.explanation: d6 attacks the e5 knight. After Nf3, Black can recover the pawn with ...Nxe4; immediate ...Nxe4 allows awkward queen pressure with Qe2.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Sacrifices a pawn for rapid development and a kingside attack; dangerous and fun, but objectively risky since it loosens White’s own king.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black holds a solid d5/e6 wall and aims to free the game with ...c5 or ...dxc4; very sturdy, but the c8 bishop can stay passive for a long time.
notes: White takes the centre with the queen pawn, supported from the start by the queen.
Black meets it head on. Now both sides have a pawn in the middle.
The Queen’s Gambit. It is not a real sacrifice: if Black grabs the pawn, White wins it back or gets a huge centre.
Declining. Black props up d5 with a pawn and keeps a rock-solid structure. The cost is that the c8 bishop is now boxed in behind its own pawns.
Develops the knight to its best square and adds a second attacker to d5.
Develops and defends d5 a second time.
Pins the f6 knight against the queen, which quietly increases the pressure on d5.
Breaks the pin by defending the knight with the bishop. A useful habit: meet a pin by defending the pinned piece or by challenging the pinner.

positions.title: Queen's Gambit: hold d5
positions.prompt: Keep the d5 pawn supported with the e-pawn in the Queen's Gambit Declined.
positions.explanation: e6 reinforces d5 and opens the dark bishop diagonal. The trade-off is a restricted c8 bishop, whose development needs attention later.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black grabs the c4 pawn and plans ...c5/...e6 to hit White’s centre; frees the pieces, but usually cedes White a lasting central space edge.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Supports d5 with the c-pawn while keeping the light bishop’s diagonal open; solid and reliable, but can be a touch passive and drawish.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: A quick, low-theory setup with Bf4/e3/c3/Bd3 that White can play on autopilot; safe and practical, but rarely fights for a real opening advantage.
notes: The queen pawn opening. If you want one 1.d4 system that needs almost no memorisation, this is it.
Black takes an equal share of the centre.
Develops toward the centre and supports d4.
Black develops the other knight and keeps the position symmetrical for now.
The move that defines the London. Crucially the bishop gets outside the pawn chain BEFORE playing e3, which would otherwise trap it behind its own pawns.
Black develops and prepares to bring the dark bishop out.
Now e3 is safe: it supports d4 and opens a path for the light bishop.
Black develops and offers a trade of the dark bishops, which would relieve some of the pressure.

A near-automatic setup. Whatever Black does, White aims for the same pieces on the same squares, then castles. That predictability is the point: you spend your thinking time on the middlegame instead of the opening.

positions.title: London: build behind the bishop
positions.prompt: Your dark bishop is already outside the pawn chain. Support d4 and free the other bishop.
positions.explanation: e3 supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop diagonal. Developing Bf4 first kept the dark bishop outside the chain.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Fianchettoes to pressure d5 and Black’s queenside along the long diagonal; strategically rich for White, but Black can hold by returning the c4 pawn at the right moment.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black cedes the centre then strikes back with ...e5 or ...c5 and a kingside pawn storm; rich attacking play, but risky if the counterattack is too slow.
notes: White takes the centre with the queen pawn. Quieter than 1.e4: lines stay closed for longer.
Black develops and eyes the centre from a distance instead of occupying it at once. This restraint is the whole idea of the King’s Indian.
White grabs more space. Two big pawns in the centre is exactly what the King’s Indian invites.
Prepares to fianchetto: the bishop is heading to g7 where it will stare down the long diagonal for the rest of the game.
Develops and adds a third attacker to the centre.
The key piece. From g7 this bishop pressures d4 and, later, the whole queenside diagonal once the centre opens.
White builds the ideal centre. Do not panic: you are letting this happen on purpose.
Controls e5 and prepares a later ...e5 pawn break. Black is ready to castle before challenging the centre.
White develops the kingside knight and adds a defender to d4. Both bishops still need development.
Castling secures the king, but the queenside pieces still need development. Black can challenge the centre with ...e5 or ...c5; the pawn structure determines the next plan.

positions.title: King's Indian: prepare counterplay
positions.prompt: White has a broad centre. Restrain e5 and prepare your own central challenge.
positions.explanation: d6 controls e5 and prepares a later ...e5 break. Black should castle and develop before deciding how to challenge White's centre.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: The main tabiya: White expands on the queenside while Black plays ...f5 to storm the king; a race where knowing your attack faster than White’s is decisive.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: White plays f3 to build a huge centre and castle long; very solid for White, but committing the king queenside gives Black a clear ...c5/...b5 or ...f5 target.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: White grabs maximum space with e4/f4; the most aggressive anti-KID try, but the over-extended centre is a target for Black’s ...c5 and ...e5 breaks.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: White fianchettoes to blunt the g7 bishop and calm the position; the safest anti-KID setup, which takes much of the sting out of Black’s kingside attack.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: The classical reply to 1.e4: fight for the centre with ...e5 and quick development; principled and flexible, but invites the whole weight of Ruy/Italian theory.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: The critical try: trade the d-pawn for the c-pawn to open lines and seize the centre; the most testing line, at the cost of learning the most theory.
notes: Your first move as a 1.e4 player: claim the centre and open lines for the queen and light bishop.
The Sicilian, and by far the most common answer to 1.e4. Black fights for the centre without symmetry: the c-pawn will trade for your d-pawn.
Develop and prepare d4. This is the standard route into the main lines.
Black supports a later ...e5 or ...e6 and keeps things flexible.
The critical break. Opening the centre while you are better developed is the whole point of the Open Sicilian.
Black must take, or White simply keeps a big centre for free.
Recapturing with the knight puts it actively in the centre. White has traded the central d-pawn for Black's c-pawn, gaining activity while Black keeps both central pawns.
Black develops with a threat: the knight attacks the e4 pawn.
Defends e4 and finishes bringing out the queenside knight. From here White usually castles and chooses a setup; Black picks a system with ...a6 (Najdorf), ...Nc6 (Classical) or ...e6 (Scheveningen).

positions.title: Sicilian: defend with development
positions.prompt: Black has attacked e4. Defend it while developing the queenside knight.
positions.explanation: Nc3 protects e4 and brings another piece into the game. White exchanged the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn to gain active development, not to win material.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black develops naturally rather than committing to ...a6 or ...g6; sound and flexible, and it invites the sharp Richter-Rauzer with Bg5.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black builds the small centre with ...d6 and ...e6 and waits to counter; very resilient, but it cedes space and invites a kingside pawn storm.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Sidesteps the whole Open Sicilian by trading on c6 for a structural edge; far less theory to learn, and the play is strategic rather than a memory race.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: The 2...d6 cousin of the Rossolimo: check first, then settle for a small, safe pull; low theory, but it hands Black easy equality if White plays too quietly.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Prepares d4 with a big pawn centre instead of the Open Sicilian; easy to learn and solid, though 2...d5 and 2...Nf6 give Black comfortable, well-charted answers.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Skips the centre trade entirely: fianchetto, f4, and attack on the kingside; almost no theory, but Black gets a free hand on the queenside.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Offers a pawn for fast development and open c- and d-files; dangerous against the unprepared, but objectively Black equalises with accurate play.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black accepts a hole on d5 for piece activity and the bishop pair; deeply analysed and fully sound, but the structural concession is permanent.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Fianchettoes a move earlier to aim for ...d5 in one go; smoother than the Dragon, but it walks into the Maroczy Bind with c4.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Flexible development that keeps ...d5 and ...Bb4 ideas open; hard to attack directly, but Black must be precise about when to commit the d-pawn.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black’s most combative Sicilian: ...a6 prepares ...e5/...b5 counterplay; hugely dynamic, but among the most theory-heavy openings in chess.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black fianchettoes and aims the g7 bishop and c-file at White’s king; razor-sharp, but White’s opposite-side Yugoslav Attack can be crushing if Black is slow.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black challenges the centre with ...d5 and plays for ...c5 breaks; very solid and strategically clear, but the c8 bishop is famously hard to develop.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Like the French but the light bishop gets out to f5 first; extremely sound with a healthy structure, at the cost of a slightly passive, slow game.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black trades in the centre at once for a simple, sturdy setup; easy to learn, but the early queen sortie costs time White can use to develop with tempo.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black pins the c3 knight to fight for e4 and often doubles White’s pawns; one of the soundest defences to 1.d4, though it can concede the bishop pair.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: A flexible reversed-Sicilian setup where White plays on the flanks; low-risk and rich in transpositions, but rarely forces an early advantage.

openings.sourceField: Standard opening theory; confirm against a primary source before marking verified.
openings.idea: Black grabs kingside space with ...f5 to play for a direct attack; ambitious and unbalancing, but the f5 push permanently weakens Black’s own king.

openings.sourceField: https://github.com/lichess-org/chess-openings/blob/master/c.tsv
openings.idea: White gains space with a pawn chain; Black attacks its base on d4 rather than accepting a cramped position.
notes: Occupies the centre and opens paths for the queen and bishop.
Prepares ...d5, but temporarily shuts in the c8 bishop.
Builds a two-pawn centre while Black prepares to challenge it.
Attacks e4 and contests the centre with a protected pawn.
Gains space and locks the centre. The e5 pawn depends on the pawn on d4.
Attacks d4, the base of the pawn chain. Undermining the support is often easier than attacking the advanced pawn.
Adds pawn support to d4, so a trade on d4 can be met by cxd4.
Develops with another attack on d4. Black can add pressure with ...Qb6 while White develops.

positions.title: French: attack the pawn chain
positions.prompt: White has gained space. Strike at the base of the central pawn chain.
positions.explanation: c5 attacks d4, which supports e5. After c3, ...Nc6 adds another attacker to d4. This is a plan to challenge the centre, not just a move to memorise.

openings.sourceField: https://github.com/lichess-org/chess-openings/blob/master/b.tsv
openings.idea: Black supports the centre with ...c6 and develops the light bishop before closing its diagonal with ...e6.
notes: Takes central space and frees the queen and light bishop.
Prepares ...d5 without closing the c8 bishop diagonal.
White takes the space Black has left available.
Challenges e4 with a pawn already supported by c6.
Locks the centre and takes space, but leaves Black time to develop the light bishop.
Gets the light bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6. Move order matters: ...e6 first would block this route.
Supports d4 and gives the centre a solid base.
Supports d5 and frees the dark bishop now that the light bishop is outside the chain.
Develops the bishop toward a safe kingside setup. White still needs to develop the g1 knight before castling.

positions.title: Caro-Kann: free the bishop first
positions.prompt: Develop the light bishop outside the pawn chain before playing ...e6.
positions.explanation: Bf5 develops the c8 bishop before ...e6 closes its diagonal. This move order keeps the bishop active despite White's space advantage.

openings.sourceField: https://github.com/lichess-org/chess-openings/blob/master/b.tsv
openings.idea: Black challenges e4 immediately; White develops with tempo against the early queen and then occupies the centre.
notes: Claims a central square and opens lines for development.
Challenges the e4 pawn immediately, inviting an exchange.
Accepts the central exchange and draws a black piece onto d5.
Recovers the pawn but exposes the queen to a developing attack.
Develops the knight and attacks the queen at the same time. White gains time because Black must respond to the threat.
Moves the queen out of attack while keeping it active along the fifth rank and a5-e1 diagonal.
Claims the centre with the remaining central pawn and opens the c1 bishop diagonal.
Develops a knight and controls e4 and d5. Both sides should finish development and secure their kings.

positions.title: Scandinavian: develop with tempo
positions.prompt: Bring a knight toward the centre while attacking the exposed queen.
positions.explanation: Nc3 develops and attacks Qd5 in one move. After ...Qa5, White can claim the centre with d4 rather than spend more time chasing the queen.

openings.sourceField: https://github.com/lichess-org/chess-openings/blob/master/a.tsv
openings.idea: Both sides control central squares from the flanks. The fianchetto develops the bishop without committing the d- or e-pawn.
notes: Controls d5 from the side while leaving the central pawns flexible.
Mirrors the structure and controls d4.
Develops a knight toward d5 and e4.
Black develops with similar central control.
Prepares Bg2, placing the bishop on the long diagonal rather than behind a central pawn.
Black prepares the same bishop development on g7.
Completes the fianchetto and adds pressure along the diagonal toward d5.
Completes the matching fianchetto. The position is balanced; central pawn breaks and development will shape the next phase.

positions.title: English: prepare the long diagonal
positions.prompt: Prepare to develop the light bishop on the long diagonal while keeping your central pawns flexible.
positions.explanation: g3 prepares Bg2. The bishop will influence central squares from the flank; White can choose a central pawn break after more development.

traps.whyBad: Nf6?? ignores the mate threat 4.Qxf7#: the queen is defended by the bishop on c4.
traps.sourceField: Classic beginner mating pattern (Scholar's Mate); verify with a primary source before marking verified.

traps.whyBad: Bxd1?? grabs the queen but allows 6.Bxf7+ Ke7 7.Nd5# (Legal’s Mate). Black must recapture instead.
traps.sourceField: Classic queen-sacrifice mate (Legal’s Mate, attributed to Sire de Legal); verify with a primary source before marking verified.

traps.whyBad: Nxe4?? (without ...d6 first) runs into 4.Qe2! and if 4...Nf6?? 5.Nc6+ wins the queen by discovered check.
traps.sourceField: Well-known Petroff opening trap; verify with a primary source before marking verified.

traps.whyBad: Nxd5?? walks into the Elephant Trap: 6...Nxd5! 7.Bxd8 Bb4+ 8.Qd2 Bxd2+ 9.Kxd2 Kxd8 leaves Black a clean piece up.
traps.sourceField: Well-known QGD trap (Elephant Trap); verify with a primary source before marking verified.
